answers.text: One instruction: return exactly three lines, in order -- delivery date, item and quantity, change from original order -- using a fixed template. Label each line (Date / Item & Qty / Change) so it's unambiguous which line is which.
Structure: submitter, date range, itemised lines (date, amount, category), total -- in that fixed order.
There's an error in this email. The call was on the 14th; the 19th is five days later, not the 'three days out' the email states.
The 15% delivery growth (54 to 62) checks out fine. The on-time rate is wrong: 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not 97%.
I'd sign off Output 2 -- it shows the source figures and the calculation. Output 1 gives no way to see the €612,000 or €25,100 it's built from.
I'd send Reply 2 -- it names the order and credit references. Reply 1 claims 'entirely our error' and a credit with no order number or reference to check it against.
1. No -- that's the customer's delivery address, personal data tied to an identifiable customer. 3. No -- next quarter's pricing is unreleased and competitively sensitive.

Unit pricing and volume discounts are sensitive -- redact the figures before pasting anything in. The confidentiality clause names both companies, which makes it a harder no than a generic clause would be.
I'd cross-cast the report's totals against the delivery log itself every week. That happens Friday, right before the report goes to the ops manager.
Step 1 -- extracting the item list and quantities -- is where an error would compound downstream. But step 4, the automatic send, is where it becomes irreversible -- that's where the gate belongs.
